name: Leave-in conditioner

lead: A leave-in conditioner is applied to damp hair after washing and not rinsed out. It keeps hair softer, smoother and easier to comb between washes, and the smoothing shows right away.

Light conditioning agents, usually cationic surfactants, silicones, humectants and oils, coat the fibre, flatten the cuticle, reduce friction and static, and leave a thin film until the next wash. It works on the surface, since hair cannot be repaired biologically, and no trials of the product category were found.

paras: Used as creams, lotions, sprays or mists on the lengths and ends after washing, daily or as needed. Some versions add heat or UV protection and are used before styling.
Considered a low-risk cosmetic. Buildup and scalp flaking are reported with heavy use or application at the roots, and individual ingredients can cause allergic reactions.

angle.text: Leave-in conditioner is applied after washing for daily softness, detangling and frizz control. The smoothing effect is visible right away and temporary, and some formulas add heat protection.

lead: A leave-in conditioner is a no-rinse hair product applied to damp (or sometimes dry) hair after washing and left in. It is sold for ongoing moisture, detangling, smoothing, frizz reduction and, in some formulas, heat protection [1][2]. Formats include creams, lotions, sprays and mists [1].

Wikipedia describes leave-in conditioners as lighter formulas than rinse-out types, often containing silicones or polymers, that reduce static and may offer some heat and UV protection [2]. Conditioners in general improve combability and appearance by reducing friction between fibres; they coat the hair rather than repair it, since hair is not living tissue [2].
No clinical trials of leave-in conditioners as a product category were found. Published research on conditioning agents is mostly laboratory testing of ingredients.
infobox: Cationic surfactants, silicones, humectants, oils, proteins

paras: Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, lists typical ingredients as humectants such as glycerin, silicones such as dimethicone, plant oils such as argan or jojoba, proteins and vitamins [1]. Wikipedia's article on conditioners names cationic surfactants (such as cetrimonium chloride), fatty alcohols, silicones, hydrolysed proteins, panthenol, humectants, acidifiers, sequestrants, UV filters and thermal protectants as typical components of conditioners generally [2].
Cationic surfactants bind to the negatively charged surface of damaged hair, flatten the cuticle and reduce static, and also provide a surface on which oils and silicones can deposit [2].

Rinse-out conditioners are applied after shampooing, left on for a few minutes and rinsed away, while leave-ins stay in the hair [1][2]. Deep conditioners or hair masks are thicker and are left on for about 20 to 30 minutes [2]. Leave-in formulas are described as lighter so that they do not weigh down hair [1].

Manufacturers and secondary sources describe benefits including less frizz, easier combing, reduced breakage, added shine and some protection from heat styling [1]. Wikipedia notes that benefits such as repair and strengthening are often advertised but are not treated as established [2]. Laboratory studies cited there include reduced combing breakage after certain polymer pretreatments before hot flat-ironing and increased break stress with panthenol in one study [2].

Product guidance summarised by Grokipedia advises applying leave-ins to mid-lengths and ends and avoiding the scalp to prevent buildup or irritation, and says dermatologists recommend washing out accumulated residue periodically [1]. Wikipedia notes that conditioner left on the scalp can dry and flake in a way that resembles dandruff [3].
No studies found. No human trials of leave-in conditioners as a product category were located; related evidence consists of ingredient-level laboratory studies of conditioning agents [2].
